title: Trihexyphenidyl

source.dataset: psychonautwiki_db.zip (psychonautwiki.db, SQLite export provided by Hany, file dated 2026-11-25)

plain_text:
Trihexyphenidyl (THP, Pacitane, Benzhexol, Trihex, Artane, and others) is an anticholinergic substance of the antimuscarinic class used to treat stiffness, tremors, spasms, and poor muscle control. In high doses, it has been reported to act as a psychedelic and deliriant. 

Trihexyphenidyl has been used for the symptomatic treatment of Parkinson's disease as approved by the FDA in the United States since 2003. It is also used for the treatment of drug-induced movement disorders such as essential tremors and akathisia, commonly caused by antipsychotics. 

History and culture

Neurologist and author Dr. Oliver Sacks reported using the drug recreationally in the 1960s, he recalled taking "a large dose" knowing full well the drug was intended for people with Parkinson's.

During the 1970s, THP (trade name Parkan) was the most popular recreational prescription drug in Hungary. In 2008, a news report mentioned that trihexyphenidyl was seen to be used for recreational purposes among Iraqi soldiers and police, stating that the drugs were taken to relieve combat stress reaction, known to cause the "thousand-yard stare." While that was the case for some, others used it as a substitute or more intense version of LSD. This was especially prevalent in the 1960s, according to a report in "The New Yorker". 

Similarly to those in Iraqi forces, some of the appeal was that the individual may retain partial control while under the influence, unlike stronger psychedelics.

Chemistry

Trihexyphenidyl can be synthesized in two ways, one linear and one convergent synthesis.

In the first way, the 2-(1-piperidino)propiophenone is synthesized in turn by the aminomethylation of acetophenone using paraformaldehyde and piperidine in a Mannich reaction. 

In the second way, the 2-(1-piperidino)propiophenone is reacted with cyclohexylmagnesium bromide in a Grignard reaction.

Pharmacology

Trihexyphenidyl is an anticholinergic. Specifically an antimuscarinic and acts as a non-selective antagonist of all five muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. However, its antagonistic activity is much stronger at the muscarinic acetylcholine M1 and M4 receptors. It is known to be selective for these receptors.

The exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, but it is known to block impulses in innervated structures like smooth muscles, salivary glands, and eyes (mydriasis). In very high doses central toxicity as seen in atropine overdose is noted.

It possibly also binds to dopamine receptors.
